name: Cognitive Load Theory
statement: Because working memory is tiny, teaching should avoid overloading it so knowledge can take root.
statementAccent: teaching should avoid overloading it so knowledge can take root
meaning: Cognitive load theory is a theory of learning and instructional design developed by the educational psychologist John Sweller, beginning in the late 1980s, which holds that instruction should be designed to respect the severe limits of human working memory. Its central premise is that working memory, the mental workspace where information is actively held and processed, can handle only a few items at a time and for a short duration, whereas long-term memory is effectively unlimited and stores organized knowledge structures called schemas. Learning, in this view, means building and refining schemas in long-term memory, and it can occur only if working memory is not overwhelmed while it happens. When too much is asked of working memory at once, it becomes overloaded and learning suffers. The theory distinguishes different sources of load on working memory: intrinsic load, the inherent difficulty of the material; extraneous load, the burden imposed by poor presentation or design, which should be minimized; and germane load, the effort devoted to building schemas. From these ideas cognitive load theory derives concrete principles for effective teaching, such as using worked examples and avoiding confusing or redundant presentations, and it has become highly influential in instructional design and educational psychology.
mechanism: Cognitive load theory rests on a model of memory in which a narrow working memory feeds a vast long-term memory. Working memory can hold only a small number of elements, classically summarized by the idea that people can keep only a few items in mind at once, and it can process novel information for only a short time before it fades, so it is the bottleneck of learning. Long-term memory, by contrast, is effectively unlimited and stores schemas, organized structures of knowledge that let a learner treat many related elements as a single chunk and recognize a problem as a familiar type. Learning is the construction and automation of these schemas, which, once formed, greatly reduce the demand on working memory because a whole schema can be handled as one unit. The theory identifies three sources of load on working memory. Intrinsic load is the built-in complexity of the material, driven by how many elements interact and must be processed together. Extraneous load is the unnecessary burden imposed by the way information is presented or by poor instructional design, and it should be minimized because it wastes limited capacity. Germane load is the productive effort devoted to processing information and constructing schemas. Effective instruction reduces extraneous load and manages intrinsic load so that working-memory capacity is freed for the germane work of learning.

examples.text: Intrinsic load is the material's inherent difficulty, extraneous load comes from poor presentation, and germane load is the effort of building schemas.
Studying worked examples instead of solving problems from scratch reduces load and helps novices build schemas more efficiently.
Once a schema is formed in long-term memory, many related elements can be handled as one unit, freeing working memory.

whyItMatters: Cognitive load theory is one of the most influential frameworks in modern educational psychology and instructional design, because it grounds teaching in the actual limits of human memory. By recognizing that working memory can process only a little at a time while long-term memory can store vast organized knowledge, it explains why learners are easily overwhelmed and why well-designed instruction matters so much. The theory turns this insight into practical, evidence-based principles for designing lessons, materials, and problems, such as using worked examples to guide novices, avoiding split attention by integrating related information, and cutting redundant content that adds load without adding learning. These principles have reshaped how textbooks, e-learning, training, and classroom teaching are designed, helping educators present complex material without overloading students. Cognitive load theory also connects the science of memory to the practice of teaching, giving instructional design a rigorous foundation. Its influence spans schools, universities, professional training, and the design of educational technology.

limits: Cognitive load theory is influential and useful, but some of its details are debated and evolving. The status and definition of germane load in particular have been reconsidered over time; in a later revision, germane load was redefined as the working-memory resources devoted to dealing with intrinsic load rather than a separate additive source, so that some formulations keep only intrinsic and extraneous load as the basic categories. The idea that the three types of load simply add up to a single total, and the practical measurement of each type, have both been questioned, with limited empirical support for a constant total load, so parts of the theory are best treated as an evolving research area rather than settled fact. The theory draws on the classic idea that working memory holds only a few items, itself an approximation.
misreadings: Cognitive load theory does not treat all mental effort as harmful; extraneous load from poor design should be cut, but germane load, the effort of building schemas, is productive. Its three types of load are not a settled, simply additive scheme, since the germane-load concept has been revised and the additivity questioned. And it is a framework for design informed by memory research, not a precise measurement instrument, so treating all load as bad, the three loads as a fixed additive formula, or the theory as exactly measurable, misreads an influential but evolving account of learning and memory.
origin: A theory of learning and instructional design developed by the educational psychologist John Sweller from the late 1980s, holding that instruction must respect the narrow limits of working memory so schemas can form in long-term memory.
